venues.d: A tiny Rosewood lodge above Lake Wakatipu — three suites and four villas in the beech forest, service to rival any city house.
A great stone-and-timber lodge on the shore of Lake Wakatipu beneath the Humboldt range — the archetype of the New Zealand high-country lodge.
An architectural marvel under a slatted timber roof in a remote high-country valley — pods and suites dissolving into the landscape.
The best few rooms in town — an 1861 lakefront landmark on Marine Parade, run as an intimate private hotel.
Standalone villas set among organic Pinot Noir vines, beside the region's original wine cave and its landmark winery.
Nine private hilltop villas with floor-to-ceiling glass framing Lake Wakatipu and the Remarkables — seclusion two miles from town.
A six-room lakeside lodge on the shore of Lake Wanaka, with its own alpine chalet high in the Buchanan range for heli-guests.
French polish in the heart of the village — the most refined full-service city hotel in Queenstown proper.
A restored 1888 Victorian villa turned eight-room boutique hotel — the grand private-residence feel, above the village.
An alpine retreat and vineyard on the shores of Lake Hayes — five-star calm between Queenstown and Arrowtown.
A design-led, playful house near the lakefront — style and a good bar at a gentler price.
Vaughan Mabee's hyper-local, wild-and-endemic tasting menu at the Amisfield winery — New Zealand's most celebrated kitchen.
Chris Scott's produce-driven cooking at the eco-minded Sherwood — much of it from the restaurant's own gardens.
Ben Bayly's ode to Northern Italy through a Central Otago lens — a stone cottage on Arrowtown's historic main street.
James Stapley's small, ever-improving Wanaka room — sharing plates that get better every year.
Josh Emett's refined bistro in a garden courtyard off the mall — polished, seasonal, and reliably excellent.
Serious steak on the waterfront — arguably the best cut in the province, done without fuss.
A stalwart of adventure-capital dining — meat, game and a vast wine list in a clubby lakefront room.
A wine-led kitchen doing considered, seasonal small plates — Queenstown's most food-and-wine-minded newcomer to the hats.

The steepest cable-car lift in the Southern Hemisphere climbs 480m in about ten minutes to a glass-fronted eyrie over Lake Wakatipu, with The Remarkables and Cecil and Walter Peaks laid out across the water. Ride up for a leisurely buffet at the Stratosfare Restaurant, or simply for the sundowner view — gentle enough for the grandparents, spectacular for everyone.

At the top of the gondola, gravity carts wind down banked, tunnelled tracks with 220-degree views of the lake and mountains — the Blue Track a gentle cruise, the Red Track steeper and faster. It is the rare thrill that a nine-year-old and a grandfather can both take on, at their own pace, side by side.

venues.n: TSS Earnslaw Steamship Cruise to Walter Peak
venues.d: The 1912 'Lady of the Lake' is the only hand-fired coal steamship still carrying passengers in the Southern Hemisphere — a 90-minute glide across the water to Walter Peak High Country Farm, engine room open to wander and a pianist on deck. At the farm, a gourmet barbecue and a sheep-shearing show delight children while elders relax by the fire; ask for the vegetarian menu in advance.

A leafy peninsula reaching into Lake Wakatipu, threaded with rose gardens, giant sequoias, a frisbee-golf course and easy flat paths right on the water — five minutes' stroll from the town centre. It is the gentle, unhurried heart of Queenstown: a picnic, a slow lakeside walk, and the mountains reflected on still mornings.

The waterfront promenade is the town's living room — jetties, the historic Steamer Wharf, lakeside restaurants and the famous Fergburger queue just up the hill. Take an evening walk as the peaks turn pink, or hand the family a lakeside table for dinner with the water at your feet.

The only operator licensed inside the sheer Shotover Canyons, these red jet boats skim inches from rock walls at 85kph and spin the signature 360s down a river no other boat can run. A thrilling but accessible half-hour — the kind of adrenaline the teenagers demand and the parents secretly love.

venues.n: Kawarau Bridge Bungy — the World's First
venues.d: AJ Hackett opened commercial bungy jumping here in 1988; the 43m leap off the historic suspension bridge into the Kawarau River is where the whole sport began. Even if no one in the family jumps, the viewing decks and cantilevered platform make it a genuine pilgrimage — watch, cheer, and photograph the leap.

Reached by 4WD across private farmland, the Nevis is New Zealand's highest bungy — a 134m plunge from a pod slung over a canyon — plus the world's biggest swing, which arcs a vast 300m and can be ridden tandem. This is the serious adventurer's badge; for the rest, the drive and the canyon setting alone are extraordinary.

A 60m freefall from a 109m clifftop platform before a giant 200m swing sweeps you over the river — jumped forwards, backwards or in one of dozens of theatrical release styles. It sits in the sweet spot between bungy and pure fun, with the milder Canyon Fox zipline alongside for those who prefer to watch.

Tandem jumps from 9,000, 12,000 or 15,000 feet fall over an almost unfair panorama — the lake, the alps and the fjords all at once. It is the once-in-a-lifetime photograph; and for family members staying on the ground, the drop zone viewing is part of the theatre.

venues.n: White-Water Rafting the Shotover & Kawarau Rivers
venues.d: The Shotover delivers grade 3–5 rapids down the legendary Skippers Canyon Road and through the dark Oxenbridge Tunnel; the Kawarau runs a gentler grade 2–3 for families and first-timers. A guided, full-day wilderness outing — choose the river to match your nerve.

venues.a: Arthurs Point, above the Shotover River
venues.d: Private cedar-lined hot tubs perched over the Shotover gorge, where a garage-style wall slides open so you soak half-inside, half under the open alpine sky. Booked room by room, it is the discreet, restorative counterpoint to a day of adventure — a couples' soak, or the whole family unwinding with the mountains in view.

Twenty-five minutes from town, Central Otago's 'Valley of the Vines' is world-famous for cool-climate Pinot Noir, its cellar doors strung along the Kawarau Gorge. A private-driver tour lets everyone taste freely — seated fireside at Amisfield, or deep inside the country's largest wine cave at Gibbston Valley — over a long, unhurried lunch.

venues.n: Gibbston Valley Winery, Wine Cave & Cheesery
venues.d: The region's oldest vineyard, first vintage 1987, is now a small estate in itself — a candlelit tasting in New Zealand's largest wine cave, an on-site cheesery, a bistro and a luxury lodge and spa. A single, elegant stop that satisfies serious wine lovers and casual visitors alike.

A rustic converted woolshed turned into one of the country's most acclaimed dining rooms, where the celebrated 'Trust the Kitchen' tasting menu is paired with the estate's own Pinot. Reserve well ahead; it is the definitive long lunch, and the kitchen handles vegetarian and dietary requests with real care.

A jewel of a settlement on the gold-bearing Arrow River, its 1860s Buckingham Street lined with more than sixty preserved miners' cottages, boutiques and cafés. A gentle, walkable day of history and browsing — with the excellent Lakes District Museum for the curious and gold-panning in the river for the children.

At the edge of town along Bush Creek stand the restored stone huts and Ah Lum's store of the Chinese gold-miners who arrived from 1866 — a quiet, moving record of a community that was pushed to the town's margins. A short, thoughtful walk that gives Arrowtown's prettiness real depth.

For a few weeks in April and May the town's avenues of oaks, poplars and sycamores blaze gold and amber — one of the most photographed sights in the South Island, crowned by the Arrowtown Autumn Festival. Time a visit here and the whole family walks through a painting.

venues.a: Head of Lake Wakatipu, 45km from Queenstown
venues.d: The road to Glenorchy is itself one of the world's great drives, hugging the lake to a tiny township at the gateway of Mt Aspiring National Park and the valley literally named Paradise. Base a serene day here among braided rivers and beech forest — the setting for Lord of the Rings' Misty Mountains and Isengard.

A jet boat threads the braided, glacier-fed Dart through the heart of a UNESCO wilderness, with 360-degree spins and a guided walk through ancient beech forest and film locations. Faster than the TSS Earnslaw but far gentler than the Shotover — a scenic thrill that spans the generations.

Guided treks cross glacial rivers and open flats beneath towering peaks, from gentle walking-pace rides for beginners to longer back-country trails. It is a soft, cinematic way into landscapes most visitors only see from a boat — well suited to a mixed-ability family group.

venues.n: Lord of the Rings 4WD Film-Location Safari (Nomad Safaris)
venues.d: A half-day 4WD tour to the real Middle-earth — the Kawarau Gorge that became the Pillars of the Kings, Deer Park Heights and The Remarkables that stood in for the Misty Mountains — with gold-panning along the way. Minimal walking and small Land Cruiser groups make it easy for every age.

A flat, beautiful 8km circuit around a mirror-still lake famous for its reflections of the surrounding hills — about two to three easy hours, or a gentle e-bike. One of the district's most relaxing outings, and a lovely stop paired with an Amisfield lunch nearby.

A hidden, horseshoe-shaped lake ringed by hills down a short gravel road, gloriously quiet and framed for still-water reflections at dawn and dusk. A peaceful picnic, an easy loop walk or a paddle — the local's antidote to the town's bustle.

A 45-minute flight over the Southern Alps and glaciers to land at Milford, cruise the fjord, and fly home — often called the world's finest scenic flight, and a fraction of the driving day. The private, elevated way to see Fiordland when time and comfort matter.

Shorter flights sweep over the lake, The Remarkables and Cecil and Walter Peaks with a snow or summit landing — a gentle taste of the high country for those not ready for a full heli-picnic. A superb way to give elders the alpine grandeur without a hike.

Gin-clear high-country rivers hold sight-fishable brown trout that can top ten pounds; a private guide walks you to spring creeks, or a helicopter drops you into pristine backcountry water no road reaches. A meditative, world-class pursuit for the angler in the family — bespoke and unhurried.

The closest field to town on a fully sealed road, with wide open runs, a strong learners' area and New Zealand's only floodlit night skiing followed by après. Between roughly June and October it is the family's easy day on the snow; out of season, the summit road still rewards with sweeping views.

The mountain range that gives Queenstown its silhouette hides sheltered basins and one of the country's best beginner zones served by covered conveyor lifts. In winter it is a superb, uncrowded family day out; the drive up alone, in any season, is spectacular.

The region's largest ski area and best all-rounder, reliably snowy, with terrain for every level and a beloved après scene — reached over the dramatic Crown Range Road, New Zealand's highest sealed pass. Worth the drive for a change of mountain, and a fine stop en route to Wanaka.

A calmer, more local-feeling lake town over the Crown Range, with a famous lone willow standing in the water, gentle waterfront walks and the quirky Puzzling World for children. An easy, pretty day trip that trades Queenstown's buzz for something more serene.

New Zealand's most photographed viewpoint — a switchbacked ridge that opens onto Lake Wanaka and the Southern Alps at your feet, about a 16km, five-to-six-hour return climb. A serious but non-technical hike for the fit; start at first light to have the famous ledge to yourselves.

venues.n: The Crown Range Road & Cardrona Hotel
venues.d: New Zealand's highest sealed road switchbacks over the Crown Range with a lookout that takes in the whole Wakatipu Basin, pausing at the 1863 Cardrona Hotel — one of the country's oldest and most photogenic pubs. A scenic drive that is a destination in itself, easy for all ages with a driver.

One of New Zealand's most dramatic and precipitous roads, cut by hand during the gold rush along sheer schist walls above the Shotover — driven only by licensed guides. A vertiginous, story-rich half-day of history and jaw-dropping scenery, no walking required.

venues.n: Queenstown Trail — E-Bike the Lakes & Vineyards
venues.d: A superb network of largely flat, sealed cycle trails links the lakefront, Lake Hayes, Arrowtown and the Gibbston wineries, with swing bridges over turquoise rivers along the way. On an e-bike it suits mixed fitness perfectly — pedal between cellar doors, with a support vehicle if you prefer.

From roughly March to October, expert astronomers set up high-powered telescopes at the gondola summit to tour the Milky Way and the Southern Cross under some of the clearest skies in the hemisphere. A calm, wonder-filled evening — and the Central Otago region as a whole holds Dark Sky status.

A guided series of ziplines and treetop platforms threads the native forest below the gondola, blending gentle thrill with a genuine conservation story and huge lake views. A crowd-pleaser that spans ages — real fun for children with an environmental lesson folded in.

Departing right from the town pier, this hour-long ride runs Lake Wakatipu and the Kawarau and Shotover Rivers with spins and speed but a milder edge than the canyon-bound Shotover Jet. The convenient, family-friendly jet-boat option — no transfer, straight off the waterfront.

venues.n: Paragliding & Tandem Hang Gliding from Bob's Peak
venues.d: Launch off the mountain above town and soar tandem over the lake with a certified pilot, floating gently down to the lakefront — the calmest way to fly, with none of the freefall. A serene, photogenic thrill for those who want the view without the adrenaline of a skydive.

The town punches far above its size on food — from the legendary Fergburger queue to fine dining, a serious craft-beer and cocktail scene, and increasingly good Indian restaurants for a taste of home. An easy, buzzy evening out; several kitchens cater well for vegetarian and Jain preferences with notice.

One of the world's most scenic courses runs along the lake beneath The Remarkables, its holes framed by schist tors and open water — playable by visitors and paired with a fine clubhouse. A gracious, low-key day for the golfer in the party, with the mountains for company.
A polished, intimate cocktail room perched over Lake Wakatipu on Steamer Wharf — the town's most decorated bar.
An 1867 lakefront institution — plush sofas, a roaring fire and Bollinger by the glass, inside the town's grande-dame hotel.
A candlelit cellar bar with a great open fire — Queenstown's serious room for whisky, wine and a quiet nightcap.
